Information since September continues to point to a solid macro backdrop—strong job gains, lower unemployment, firm household spending, and inflation near 2 percent—supporting the decision to hold the federal funds rate at 2 to 2-1/4 percent while signaling further gradual increases and continuing balance-sheet normalization.

Beige Book insights reinforce this with most districts reporting consumer spending increasing at a solid pace and widespread labor tightness leading to wage gains. At the same time, firms cited labor shortages constraining operations and growth across several districts (including manufacturing), and price pressures were mixed, with reports of higher fuel and input costs. These observations are consistent with robust demand but highlight capacity and cost headwinds that could temper momentum.

In parallel, the SLOOS points to emerging credit headwinds (tighter standards for C&I and construction/land development loans and softer demand in construction lending), aligning with the moderation in business fixed investment. The Financial Stability Report’s notes on elevated valuations and rising business leverage, while overall vulnerabilities remain moderate, keep risks “roughly balanced,” albeit with a slightly more cautious tilt than headline macro data alone would suggest.
